newsitem.title: CHINA: U.S. touts open communications market in China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. touts open communications market in China.

text.p: The United States has moved to open a long-delayed cross-Pacific communications dialogue with the visit to China by officials touting the benefits of an open market, U.S. communications chief Reed Hundt said on Wednesday.

Washington was also pushing for legislative clarity in the world's potential biggest communications market and hoped to bring new balance to the Sino-U.S. telecom relationship, said Hundt, who is chairman of the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC).

"Within a decade, China will be a larger market than the United States for any kind of commmunications service, barring calamities that we don't foresee and don't hope for," Hundt told reporters in Beijing.

Hundt's visit, delayed for more than a year because of Sino-U.S. friction over Beijing's arch-rival Taiwan, was aimed at showing China the benefits to be gained from competition, market openness and regulatory clarity, he said.
"We believe that one of the outcomes of this meeting will be some concrete commitments to continuing discussions," he said. "'Better later than never' was the way we felt about this trip."

China's telecommunications network has been struggling to keep up with roaring economic growth fuelled by almost two decades of reform, making the huge potential market a tempting target for international telecommunications firms.

Telecommunications Minister Wu Jichuan said last year that foreign investment was welcome but Beijing was unlikely to ease a ban on foreign ownership or operation of telecommunications services this decade, despite rocketing demand.

Potential U.S. investors were keen to be part of China's communications revolution but wanted to be directly involved in the running of their investments, Hundt said, adding that regulatory confusion was a major worry.
"They are saying that their biggest concern about developing in China is that they have trouble understanding what the rules are," he said.

The FCC, which is responsible for regulating U.S. broadcasting and wireless, cable, satellite and telephone communications, was also hoping to start talks on the largely one-way flow of Sino-U.S. telephone traffic, he said.
Calls from the United States outnumbered those originating in China by around four to one because of the high cost of cross-Pacific calls originating in China, he said.
Under international agreements mandating a fixed charge per minute to be paid by the originating telecommunications provider, the imbalance was boosting the U.S. trade deficit, he said.
U.S. telecommunications companies paid more than $100 million a year to China out of a total deficit estimated at around $5 billion in 1996, FCC officials said.
"We end up sending much more money to China than we would want," Hundt said. "As telecoms boom in China this problem could become a very big problem."
Aside from meeting Telecommunications Minister Wu and other senior leaders, Hundt was also to meet legislators drafting China's new telecommunications law, he said.
Washington believed that the U.S. recipe of deregulation and vigorous competition was apt not just for the United States but also for other countries, he said.
"The rules can be the same rules. Economics is economics in all countries, chemistry is chemistry, physics is physics and interconnectivity is interconnectivity," Hundt said.
Beijing has long been concerned with building a world-class industrial economy, but China could also develop a competitive information-age economy, Hundt said.
"It's post-industrial talk that I'm talking here," he said.
